messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Weber, a 46-year-old graphic designer, came to treatment more than a year after an encounter with police that he still could not tell in a straight line. He described being pulled over late one evening while driving home from work after staying late on a deadline. What began as a traffic stop escalated quickly. He remembered the flash of police lights in his rearview mirror, officers shouting over one another, being ordered out of the car, and then being forced to the ground before he understood what was happening. His cheek was pressed into the pavement; he saw blood on his own hand and, in a fragment that stayed especially vivid, the torn skin and swelling on his wrist afterward. What he could never reconcile was the sense that he had done nothing to deserve it. From the start he had come to believe that what happened to him was profoundly unjust and that no one had been held accountable, and this belief hardened into a broader conviction that the trauma had ruined his life and drained it of meaning.

That sense of unfairness seemed to make the reminders of the event feel even more charged. Police uniforms, a patrol car on the street, even seeing officers standing outside a coffee shop could jolt him immediately. Visible injuries on other people had a similar effect: a cut on a coworker’s hand, a bruised face in a news image, even the exposed scrape on a stranger’s knee could grip his attention. He also complained of unwanted thoughts arriving on their own, as if his mind were ambushing him. Because he was already carrying the belief that his life had been destroyed by something that should never have happened, these reminders did not feel neutral or containable; they landed as proof that the danger and the wrongness of it were still present.

When he was triggered, the memory did not come back as a narrative he could reflect on. It arrived full force and without warning. He said that a glimpse of an officer’s badge or someone’s fresh stitches could bring back the whole scene in an instant, and when that happened he became so emotionally overwhelmed that he had to shut down the attempt to think or speak. In session he would begin describing the stop, get as far as the command to step out of the car, and then lose the thread, staring at the floor, unable to continue. His convictions about the trauma seemed to feed this as well: because he experienced the event as the moment his life was destroyed, remembering it felt less like recalling the past than being thrown back into the worst meaning of the present.

Over the months that followed, Daniel began living as though another sudden confrontation could happen at any time. He was unable to relax even in places he knew were safe. In restaurants he scanned for exits before he could settle into his chair; in his design studio he automatically noted the back stairwell and loading door. His body remained tense and ready, shoulders tight, jaw set, as though bracing had become permanent. Triggers pushed him into this state quickly, but his own beliefs sustained it too: if life had already been wrecked once by an arbitrary abuse of authority, he felt foolish letting his guard down now. The memory and the sense of current danger intensified each other. Once the scene was activated in his mind, his body reacted as if he were back on the pavement; and because his body was already on alert so much of the time, the memory seemed closer to the surface, easier to ignite.

To manage this, Daniel increasingly organized his life around not giving his mind any room. After work he disappeared into his phone, internet videos, and games for hours at a time, telling himself that if he kept his attention occupied he would not have to see the scene again. He pulled back from friends and avoided people whenever he could, preferring to sit alone in a dark room scrolling late into the night rather than risk conversation that might touch the event or put him near strangers. These habits brought immediate relief, but the relief never lasted. The more he trained himself to escape into screens and stay away from people, the less practiced he became at tolerating the memory when it broke through, and the more suddenly it seemed to hit. His world also became narrower and more filled with the very cues he feared: online news feeds exposed him to images of injuries and police footage, and going out less made every necessary outing feel more loaded, so that spotting an officer near his office building could send his body surging before he even crossed the street.

By the time he sought help, the impact had reached both home and work. He was still producing enough as a designer to get by, but he worked in isolation, avoided collaborative meetings when possible, and spent breaks hiding with his phone rather than joining coworkers. At home, his wife had begun telling him that he was present in body only, unreachable behind a screen and always watching the room. What finally brought him in was the realization that he could no longer pass a police officer or see an injured person without feeling instantly pulled back, flooded, and physically primed to flee. He said he was afraid that this was all that remained of him now, but he still hoped there might be some way to remember what happened without being overtaken by it.
